reflection of the calm and undeviating processes of nature
in the struggles of passion and the tragic climaxes of history.
For in this sphere it is not true as it is in the world of nature
that all maturity and decay bear the seeds of new life, that
death is only a transition to a new upsurge of life, that the
face of the earth constantly renews itself and at each new
springtime is arrayed with the undimmed brilliance with
which it shone on the first morning of creation. It cannot be
said of man's history:
"And all your noble works are grand
As if on that first day, creation's dawn, they stand."
It is very significant that the great German poet who was
most genuinely and deeply sensitive to the lavish beauties
and mighty energies of nature, who felt most intensely the
deity present in nature and whose poetry expresses a mystical
pantheism, that Goethe was only able to achieve these
exalted feelings by consciously averting his gaze from the
terrible abysses in the nature of man and from the madness
and folly which everywhere runs like a dark thread through
the course of human history; that he wrote Iphigenia as if no
stocking-weavers hungered in Apolda; that he did not feel
himself equal to the task of writing a true tragedy because he
felt that it would shatter the calm of his own life.
Goethe's nature-piety had seriousness and sincerity. He
was aware of the abyss whose edge he skirted. But for most
men nature-piety means nothing more than a mood of
sentimentality, because it is but the enjoyment of an hour
which remains without any abiding repercussions on their
life.
For in truth the history of man is woven with tragedy,
passion and guilt, it is stained with every horror and un-
cleanness. And in contrast with it, nature is a sphere of peace,
luminous, clear and innocent. If we identify God and nature,
then the rest of life necessarily becomes for us void of God,
surrendered to a mysterious fate, to godless passions or to the
